issues.legal_issue: The adjudicating authority’s review of a resolution plan approved by the creditors is limited and does not permit it to substitute or modify the creditors’ commercial decisions.
material_facts: The creditors approved the resolution plan by 97.36% of the voting share.
The adjudicating authority approved the plan with modifications, including changes concerning a dissenting financial creditor, the land-providing authority, and unclaimed fixed-deposit claims.
The resolution applicant and other stakeholders challenged aspects of the approval order, including the adjudicating authority’s power to modify the plan.
issues.conclusion: The adjudicating authority may review a creditors-approved plan only within the limits set by the Code. It cannot review the merits of the creditors’ commercial decisions or substitute or modify commercial terms. If the plan falls short of the applicable statutory parameters, the authority may return it to the creditors for reconsideration and resubmission.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 30(2) and 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 confine the adjudicating authority’s review to compliance with statutory requirements, including payment priorities, post-approval management, and effective implementation. Sections 32 and 61(3) limit appeals against approval orders to specified grounds. The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is not subject to merits review. Under Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Limited v. Satish Kumar Gupta, a plan that does not meet the relevant parameters may be sent back to the creditors for resubmission; K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank and Maharashtra Seamless Limited v. Padmanabhan Venkatesh likewise establish the limited scope of review and reject judicial substitution of commercial judgment.

predicates.resolution_plan_approval_review: The proceeding concerns review of a resolution plan submitted for approval after a corporate insolvency resolution process.
predicates.plan_approved_by_creditors: The creditors approved the resolution plan by the required voting majority.

issues.definition: When a creditors-approved plan is under review, the reviewing authority checks statutory compliance but does not replace the creditors’ commercial judgment or rewrite the plan.

issues.legal_issue: Creditors may consider and vote simultaneously on multiple compliant resolution plans when no applicable rule prohibits that process.
material_facts: Two resolution applicants submitted revised plans for consideration by the creditors.
The creditors considered and voted on both plans at the same time, approving one of them.
At the time of the vote, no prohibition on simultaneous voting appeared in the governing process.
A later amendment expressly provided for simultaneous voting on multiple plans.
issues.conclusion: The simultaneous voting did not vitiate approval of the selected resolution plan; the objection was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 30(3) and 30(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code require compliant plans to be presented to the Committee of Creditors for consideration and provide for approval by the requisite voting share. Regulation 39 of the CIRP Regulations did not, at the relevant time, prohibit simultaneous voting on multiple plans. The later amendment expressly providing for that procedure was treated as clarificatory. The Court also relied on its prior direction that the two eligible applicants could submit revised plans for consideration.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_resolution_process: The proceeding is a corporate insolvency resolution process in which creditors consider resolution plans.
predicates.multiple_compliant_plans_presented_to_cr: More than one plan meeting the applicable requirements was presented to the creditors for consideration.
predicates.no_rule_barred_concurrent_voting: The governing process contained no rule barring creditors from voting on multiple qualifying plans at the same time.

issues.definition: When multiple qualifying plans are presented in a corporate insolvency resolution process and concurrent voting is not barred, voting on them together does not invalidate the plan selected by the creditors.
